✅ Total Rate Cuts Since Feb 2025: 100 Basis Points
The RBI has cumulatively cut the repo rate by 100 bps (1 percentage point) in this easing cycle — from 6.50% to 5.25%. The June 2026 pause is the first after a full year of intermittent easing, signalling that the MPC is now in a data-dependent watchful mode rather than an easing mode.
⚖️ Section 3 — What Does 'Neutral' Stance Mean?
The MPC has retained its 'neutral' monetary policy stance. Understanding what this means — and why it matters — is crucial for interpreting the RBI's forward guidance.
🔴 'Accommodative' Stance (Until Jun 2025)
Signalled MPC's bias towards further rate cuts. Each decision leant toward easing monetary conditions to support growth. Rate hikes were off the table.
🟡 'Neutral' Stance (Since Jun 2025)
No pre-committed direction. The MPC can move rates either up or down — or hold. The next step depends entirely on incoming inflation, growth, and external data. Both tightening and easing remain live options.

passages.title: RBI Holds Repo Rate at 5.25% in June 2026, Retains Neutral Stance Amid Inflation Risks
passages.text:
📝 Bottom Line — Reading Between the Lines of the June 2026 Pause
The RBI's June 5, 2026 decision to hold the repo rate at 5.25% while retaining the neutral stance is fundamentally a message of watchful caution in the face of simultaneous supply-side shocks. The 100 bps of rate cuts delivered since February 2025 are still working their way through the economy — and the MPC wisely chose not to add more easing into a period of genuine inflation risk. The core message from Governor Sanjay Malhotra is clear: India's growth story remains intact at 6.6%, but the path of inflation — particularly the risk of Q3 FY27 readings touching the 6% upper band — requires close monitoring before any further easing can be considered. For borrowers, the current rate environment remains supportive relative to the 2022–2024 cycle. For investors in fixed income, the pause signals that the easy gains from rate-driven bond rally may be behind us. The August 3–5 meeting will be the next critical test — and the MPC's ability to hold the neutral stance will depend heavily on how the West Asia conflict, the monsoon, and global supply chains evolve in the weeks ahead.
